[I'll start with this.](https://youtu.be/V1YRu2pqK3g) The percussion that kicks in for the second version of Ryoshima Coast is absolutely fantastic. Nearly all the music in Okami was pretty memorable but Ryoshima Coast's themes stick out the most in my mind.

My favorite recently is Metal Gear Solid 5, but my favorite of all time is probably Halo 3. I love the way the music moves the story forward without distracting from it, and adds fervor to events like

The Metal Gear Solid series has generally been outstanding for soundtracks, yeah. (yes I know it was only in the trailer, still good) Heard a lot of good things about the music in the Halo series (never actually played any of the Halo games though, that's what I get for being a Sony fanboy).

Yeah, the best thing about a good video game soundtrack is that they're usually original creations, rather than just using popular music of the day. That lets them mesh with the story far better than other music, and creates an atmosphere unique to that game. Good discussion question!

There are times when I think popular music being part of a game's soundtrack works for it (the Grand Theft Auto series is an obvious example of this), but by and large you get a better fit with original compositions, yeah.
Like, in GTA: San Andreas, tuning the car radio to Radio Los Santos fit the atmosphere of the game nearly flawlessly in my opinion.

Yeah, and it works especially well for games that are trying to capture a certain era or location like GTA often does. I know movies and video games aren't direct analogs, but I see a similar effect with movie soundtracks: movies like "Guardians of the Galaxy" and "Watchmen" use carefully selected songs to set atmosphere and capture the essence of an era, where other films like "Star Wars" and "Jurassic Park" do much better with original creations. I guess there really isn't a rule of thumb when it comes to art, it just depends on how much effort and detail goes into the selection/creation.

GTA used more or less the same approach as The Wire. Most of the ambient music is from things you'd expect music from like clubs, cars, and boom boxes with little additional soundtrack to make up the rest and it makes sense because that's just how it is in the real world.
